newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania votes again, Socialists set for landslide.
newsitem.headline: Albania votes again, Socialists set for landslide.

text.p: Albanians went to the polls on Sunday for the second time in a week, to finalise results of elections called to heal the wounds of a rebellion that wrecked Europe's poorest country and left more than 1,500 dead.
With the former opposition Socialists already runaway winners after last Sunday's first round of voting, turnout was low in the runoff polls for undecided seats and polling stations calm.

The Socialists, reformed heirs to Albania's hardline communists, won over 80 of 155 assembly seats in the first vote on June 29, but the issue remaining on Sunday was the size of their majority over President Sali Berisha's Democrats, who had ruled since 1992.
Around 500,000 of Albania's 3.4 million people were scheduled to vote in 34 districts where no candidate managed to win an overall majority in the first round.
"But turnout is much lower than last week," said Nazmi Kucu, chairman of a polling station in central Tirana. "People are indifferent now. They are tired of it all."

The collapse early this year of popular pyramid savings funds, which angry Albanians accused Berisha and his government of allowing to flourish, ignited riots and then armed anarchy across the country.

The first round of voting was declared "adequate and acceptable" by the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe which, together with the Council of Europe, had about 450 observers monitoring the Balkan nation's election.

A 7,000-strong International Protection Force sent to Albania in April has also helped to guard polling stations to ensure the country's fourth multi-party election since the 1990 fall of communism ran smoothly.
Two Albanian monitors touring Tirana's poll booths on Sunday said only 20-25 percent of voters turned up by midday for the second round of voting, compared to over 50 percent a week earlier.
"People are not so concerned because the Democrats have already lost," pensioner Sali Spahiu told Reuters as he voted in central Tirana.
OSCE spokesman Mark Smith said voting was calm. Polling booths opened at 7am and closed at 6pm, guarded by armed police who were sweltering in 35 degree Celsius heat.
The only reported incident was police stopping an armed man from entering a booth at Kavaje, 50 km (30 miles) southwest of Tirana. The man was turned away and left peacefully.

"We have received some complaints from party officers (of both sides) about things that have allegedly occurred or allegedly will occur but none of these things have been confirmed," Smith told reporters.
He said the OSCE had no idea when the results of the second round of voting would be announced. The OSCE still does not have the final results of the first round of voting.

The runoff ballots will determine whether the Socialists, along with their leftist allies the Social Democrats and the Democratic Alliance, will gain a two-thirds majority that would enable them to get important legislation through parliament -- and vote in a new head of state.

Berisha has already said he would stand down when a new leftish government is installed. Socialist leader Fatos Nano declined to comment on a successor but local media have speculated on Socialist Party Secretary General Rexhep Mejdani.
Nano said he would be the next prime minister and his Socialist colleague, Bashkim Fino, who was appointed interim prime minister in March, would be at his "right side".
